title: Root-to-Leaf Paths With a Total
statement:
You get the root of a binary tree and an integer target. Find every path that starts at the root, goes down one child at a time and ends at a leaf (a node with no children), where the node values on the path add up to target.

Return each such path as the list of its values from root to leaf. Return the paths in any order. Two paths that pass through different nodes count separately, even if their values are the same.

Values can be negative, so a running sum above the target can still come back down.

examples.why: 5 + 3 + 1 = 9 and 5 + 8 − 4 = 9. On the right side the sum is 13 after two nodes, above the target, and the −4 still brings it back. Stopping early there would miss a path.
The root alone sums to 1, but the root has a child, so it is not a leaf. The only root-to-leaf path is 1 → 2, which sums to 3.
An empty tree has no paths at all, not even an empty one.

hints: You have to look at every root-to-leaf path. What do you need to carry down the tree so that, at a leaf, you can tell whether this path works?
Carry the running sum and the list of values on the current path. At a leaf, check the sum. Because values can be negative, you cannot prune a branch just because the sum got too big.
Use one shared path list: push the node's value before visiting its children and pop it after. At a matching leaf, save a copy of the list, not the list itself.

explain.intuition:
Walk the tree depth-first, the same way you would walk a nested menu to list every full breadcrumb trail. On the way down keep the current trail and its sum. When you reach a leaf, the trail is a complete root-to-leaf path, and you only need to compare its sum to the target.

Building a new list for every node wastes memory. Instead keep one list and treat it as a stack: push a value when you enter a node, pop it when you leave. That is backtracking. The only place you must copy is when you save an answer, because the shared list keeps changing afterwards.
steps: Start a depth-first walk at the root with an empty path and a running sum of 0.
At each node, add its value to the sum and push it onto the path.
If the node is a leaf and the sum equals target, save a copy of the path.
Otherwise recurse into the left and right children.
Before returning from the node, pop its value from the path.
pitfalls: Saving the shared path list itself instead of a copy. Every saved answer then ends up as the same, finally empty, list.
Checking the sum at nodes that still have one child. A path must end at a leaf, so [1, 2] with target 1 has no answer.
Pruning when the running sum passes the target. Negative values can bring it back down, as in the first example.

complexity.time: O(n · h): every node is visited once, and each saved path costs up to h to copy
complexity.space: O(h) for the path and recursion, plus the output

solutions.title: Explicit stack carrying whole paths
solutions.idea: Push (node, path so far, sum so far) onto a stack. Each child gets its own copy of the path, so nothing needs undoing.

solutions.title: Backtracking with one shared path
solutions.idea: Recurse depth-first. Push the value on entry, pop it on exit, and copy the path only when a leaf matches.

followups: Count paths with the target sum that may start and end at any node, as long as they go downwards. How does a prefix-sum map help?
The tree is 100 000 nodes deep, a single chain. What breaks, and how do you rewrite the walk?
